Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 1, verse 1:

Al-Basmalah

Explanation of the words:

Al-basmalah (the basmalah): the servant's saying: "Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim" (In the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful).

Al-ism (the name): a word set as a sign for a named thing, by which it is known and distinguished from others.

Allah: a proper name for the essence of the Lord, blessed and exalted, by which He is known.

Ar-Rahman: one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, derived from mercy, indicating its abundance in Him, the Exalted.

Ar-Rahim: a name and attribute of Allah, the Exalted, derived from mercy; its meaning is the One full of mercy toward His servants, bestowing it upon them in this world and the Hereafter.

The meaning of the basmalah:

"I begin my recitation seeking blessing through the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful, seeking His help, Mighty and Majestic is He."

The ruling on the basmalah:

It is prescribed for the servant, and it is required of him, that he say the basmalah at the beginning of the recitation of every surah of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, except at the recitation of Surah at-Tawbah, for he does not say the basmalah there. And if he is in an obligatory prayer, he says it silently if the prayer is one recited aloud.

It is recommended (sunnah) for the servant to say "Bismillah" when eating and drinking, and when putting on a garment; upon entering and leaving the mosque; when mounting a riding animal; and at every matter of importance.

It is also obligatory upon him to say "Bismillah, Allahu akbar" at the slaughtering and the sacrificing.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 1, verse 2:

Explanation of the words:

Al-hamd (praise): describing someone with beauty, and extolling the one who is praised for his virtues and bounties, like praise (madh) and gratitude (shukr).

Lillah (to Allah): the lam is a preposition, and its meaning is entitlement (al-istihqaq), i.e., Allah is entitled to all praises. And "Allah" is a proper name (ʿalam) for the Essence of the Lord, blessed and exalted.

Al-Rabb (the Lord): the Master, the Owner, the Reformer, the one worshipped with right, may His majesty be glorified.

Al-ʿalamin (the worlds): plural of ʿalam (world), which is everything other than Allah, Exalted is He, such as the world of the angels, the world of the jinn, the world of mankind, the world of animals, and the world of plants.

The meaning of the verse:

He, Exalted is He, informs that all kinds of praise, of attributes of majesty and perfection, belong to Him alone, to the exclusion of anyone else, since He is the Lord and Creator and Owner of everything.

And that it is incumbent upon us to praise Him and extol Him for that.

The explanation of these two words has already been given in the basmala (the invocation "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"). They are two names used as descriptions of the Name of Majesty, "Allah," in His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. This is praise of God Most High, because He alone deserves all praise.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 1, verse 4:

Explanation of the words:

Māliki (مالِك): al-Mālik: the possessor of dominion, who disposes of it as He wills.

Maliki (مَلِكِ): al-Malik: the one possessing authority, who commands and forbids, who gives and withholds, with none able to hinder Him and none able to contend with Him.

Yawmi al-din (يومَ الدين): the Day of Recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection, when Allah recompenses every soul for what it has earned.

Meaning of the verse:

A glorification of Allah, the Exalted, that He is the Owner of everything on the Day of Resurrection, a Day on which no soul possesses anything for another soul, and the Sovereignty which has no sovereign on the Day of Resurrection other than Him.

Guidance from the verses:

In these three verses there is the following guidance:

1- That Allah, the Exalted, loves to be praised, so He praised Himself and commanded His servants to do so.

2- That praise is due to a reason; otherwise it is vain and falsehood. So when Allah praised Himself, He mentioned the basis of the praise, which is that He is Lord of the worlds, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, and Master of the Day of Judgement.

Explanation of the words:

Iyyaka (إياك): a pronoun in the accusative case, used to address one person.

Na'budu (نعبد): we obey, with the utmost submission, humility, exaltation and love for You.

Nasta'in (نستعين): we seek Your help in our obedience to You.

The meaning of the verse:

Allah, exalted is He, taught us how to draw near to Him in order to have our supplications accepted. So He said: praise Allah, extol Him and glorify Him, and commit yourselves to worshipping Him alone without associating anything with Him, and seek His help and do not seek help from anyone else.

The guidance of the verse:

Among the guidance in this verse is the following:

1. The etiquette of supplication: the one who asks should precede his supplication with praise of Allah, extolling Him and glorifying Him. The Sunnah has added sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ). Then he should ask for his need, and it will be answered.

2. That one should not worship other than his Lord, and should not seek help from anyone other than Him, glorified and exalted is He.

Explanation of the Words:

Ihdina: Guide us, and continue our guidance.

As-Sirat: The path that leads to Your pleasure and Your Paradise, which is Islam for You.

Al-Mustaqim: That in which there is no deviation from the truth and no swerving from guidance.

The Meaning of the Verse:

Taught by Allah, the Most High, the servant says, among his brethren the believers, asking his Lord after having approached Him through His praise, extolling Him, glorifying Him, and pledging to Him that he and his believing brethren will worship none but Him and seek help from none but Him. They ask Him to continue guiding them to Islam so that they never cease to be guided by it.

Lessons from the Verse:

Encouragement to call upon Allah, to humble oneself before Him, and, in the hadith, "Supplication is worship" (the hadith is recorded by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah).

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 1, verse 7:

﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾

Explanation of the words:

al-Sirat (the path): its explanation has already been given.

Alladhina an'amta 'alayhim (those upon whom You have bestowed favour): they are the prophets, the truthful (al-siddiqun), the martyrs (al-shuhada') and the righteous (al-salihun), and everyone upon whom God has bestowed favour by faith in Him, knowledge of Him, knowledge of what He loves and what He abhors, and success in doing what He loves and avoiding what He dislikes.

Meaning of the verse:

When the believer asked, for himself and for his brothers, guidance to the straight path, and the path was stated in general terms, he clarified it by saying: the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour. It is the upright way that leads the servant to the good pleasure of God Almighty and to Paradise, which is Islam, resting upon faith, knowledge and action, together with avoiding polytheism and sins.

Guidance from the verse:

Among the guidance of the verse is the following:

1- Acknowledging the blessing.

2- Seeking good exemplars.

﴿other than the path of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾

Explanation of the words:

Ghayr (other than): a word used for exception, like illa (except).

Al-maghdubi 'alayhim (those who have earned anger): those upon whom God's anger has descended because of their disbelief and their corruption on earth, such as the Jews.

Al-dallin (those who are astray): those who have strayed from the road of truth and worshipped God with what He did not prescribe, such as the Christians.

Meaning of the verse:

When the believer asked his Lord for the straight path and clarified it as the path of those He has favoured with the blessing of faith, knowledge and action, and in earnestness in seeking guidance to the truth, and out of fear of going astray, he excepted from it the path of those who have earned anger and of those who are astray.

Guidance from the verse:

Among the guidance of the verse:

Encouragement to follow the way of the righteous, and warning against the way of those who go astray.

[First note]: The word "Amin" is not part of al-Fatiha. It is recommended that the imam say it after reciting al-Fatiha, prolonging his voice with it, and that the follower (al-ma'mum) say it, and the one praying alone likewise, following the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "When the imam says 'Amin', then you say 'Amin'." That is, say "Amin", meaning "O God, answer our supplication." It is also recommended to say it aloud, based on the hadith of Ibn Majah: "The Prophet (ﷺ), when he said 'not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray', would say 'Amin' until those in the first row could hear it, and the mosque would resound with it." [Second note]: Reciting al-Fatiha is obligatory in every rak'a of the prayer. As for the one praying alone and the imam, there is no disagreement on this. As for the follower, the majority of jurists hold that it is recommended for him to recite it in the silent prayers but not in the audibly recited ones, based on the hadith: "Whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation," and this specifies the general sense of the hadith: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book."
